When the same subjects are measured twice — before/after a treatment, baseline vs follow-up — a
**paired boxplot** with a line connecting each subject across the two timepoints tells the story a
plain boxplot can't. This post builds one in R by wrapping a
[ggpubr](https://rpkgs.datanovia.com/ggpubr/) `ggpaired` plot with
[canvasXpress](https://canvasxpress.org), so it becomes interactive and reproducible without
re-specifying anything.

## Install

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("canvasXpress", "ggpubr"))
```

## A paired dataset

Long format, two rows per subject — one per timepoint. Swap in your own repeated-measures table.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)

set.seed(7)
n  <- 25
df <- data.frame(
  id    = rep(paste0("P", seq_len(n)), 2),
  time  = rep(c("Baseline", "Week 12"), each = n),
  value = c(rnorm(n, 8, 1.2),                       # baseline
            rnorm(n, 8, 1.2) + rnorm(n, -1.2, 0.8)) # follow-up (a drop)
)
```

## Build it with ggpaired, then wrap it

`ggpaired` draws the two boxes and the per-subject connecting lines; `stat_compare_means` adds a
paired test. Then hand the whole thing to `canvasXpress()`:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(canvasXpress)

g <- ggpaired(
  df, x = "time", y = "value", id = "id",
  color = "time", line.color = "gray", line.size = 0.3
) +
  stat_compare_means(paired = TRUE, method = "t.test")

canvasXpress(g)
```

Each grey line is one subject moving from Baseline to Week 12, the boxes summarize each timepoint,
and the paired t-test labels the comparison. It's interactive — hover a line to follow a subject —
and the figure is one portable spec you can reproduce from R, Python or JavaScript.

## Why paired, not two independent boxes

A side-by-side boxplot hides *who* changed. The connecting lines make within-subject change visible:
a treatment can lower the group median while a handful of subjects still rise — exactly the pattern
you want to catch before drawing conclusions.
